abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework termed Predictive Manifold Coding (PMC) that fundamentally reconceptualizes neural information processing in biological neural systems. Unlike conventional rate-based coding theories that focus on firing rate modulations, PMC proposes that neural populations encode information through the geometry of attractor dynamics on low-dimensional manifolds embedded in high-dimensional neural state space. We mathematically characterize these predictive manifolds using tools from differential topology and show that neural trajectories naturally converge to these structures during cognitive processing. The framework provides a unified explanation for diverse experimental observations in computational neuroscience, including winner-take-all dynamics, persistent activity during working memory, and context-dependent coding. Furthermore, we demonstrate that PMC offers a parsimonious account of neural plasticity mechanisms, where synaptic modifications serve to shape the geometry of predictive manifolds rather than store discrete representations. Simulation results on benchmark cognitive tasks validate that PMC-based network architectures achieve comparable performance to deep learning approaches while exhibiting superior robustness to noise and superior generalization from limited examples. This paradigm shift from representation-centric to dynamics-centric neural coding theory opens new avenues for understanding brain function and inspires next-generation neuromorphic computing architectures.

We present a significantly enhanced theoretical analysis of spiking neural network learning algorithms that addresses critical limitations in existing synaptic plasticity rules. Building upon the established spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) framework, we introduce the Adaptive Temporal Window (ATW) rule, which dynamically modulates the spike pairing window based on firing statistics and neuromodulatory signals. The proposed ATW-STDP rule incorporates a mathematically rigorous formulation that ensures weight boundedness and eliminates the saturation problems inherent in classical exponential STDP models. We prove analytically that the ATW-STDP rule drives synaptic weights toward configurations that maximize mutual information between input patterns and output spike trains, establishing a principled connection between synaptic plasticity and information-theoretic optimization objectives. Extensive mathematical analysis reveals that the adaptive window mechanism naturally implements reward-modulated learning without requiring separate neuromodulatory pathways. Numerical simulations on pattern recognition tasks demonstrate that networks trained with ATW-STDP achieve 23% higher classification accuracy and 40% faster convergence compared to standard STDP, while exhibiting superior robustness to temporal noise in neural coding. This work provides both theoretical foundations and practical tools for developing more biologically plausible and computationally efficient spiking neural network models.

This paper presents the design and experimental validation of a novel neuromorphic computing architecture called Hierarchical Asynchronous Pulse Processor (HASP) that fundamentally departs from conventional clock-driven neuromorphic systems. HASP implements a truly event-driven paradigm where computation emerges solely from asynchronous neural spike events without any global synchronization signals. The architecture employs a biologically-inspired cortical column organization with hierarchical feature extraction stages that process visual information through competing and cooperating spiking neural populations. A key innovation lies in the on-chip learning module that implements a novel combination of homeostatic plasticity mechanisms and structural plasticity for automatic network adaptation. The fabricated HASP chip in 28nm CMOS technology achieves unprecedented energy efficiency of 4.2 pJ per synaptic operation while processing visual patterns at 10,000 frames per second equivalent throughput. Real-world validation on brain-computer interface applications demonstrates successful decoding of motor intentions from neural signals with latency under 5ms. The HASP architecture supports online learning and adaptation without external computation resources, representing a paradigm innovation toward truly autonomous intelligent systems. This work bridges the gap between biological neural systems and practical neuromorphic hardware, enabling deployment of neural processing capabilities in energy-constrained embedded applications.

We present substantial improvements to a brain-computer interface (BCI) system for neural decoding, achieving significantly enhanced performance through innovations in both neural signal processing and pattern recognition algorithms. The proposed system introduces a novel multi-scale temporal feature extraction pipeline that captures neural dynamics across different timescales relevant to motor and cognitive processes. Building upon existing Utah array interfaces, we develop an improved signal conditioning frontend with adaptive noise cancellation that increases signal-to-noise ratio by 35% compared to conventional designs. The core pattern recognition module employs an enhanced reservoir computing architecture with biologically-inspired read-out layers that leverage temporal attention mechanisms for improved classification of complex neural states. Extensive validation across 15 subjects performing reaching and grasping tasks demonstrates that the improved BCI system achieves 94.2% intention classification accuracy with mean decoding latency of 28ms, representing a 41% improvement in accuracy and 52% reduction in latency over state-of-the-art systems. The closed-loop performance metrics further show that users can achieve stable control with significantly reduced calibration time of only 3 minutes. These improvements advance practical deployment of neural prosthetic devices by addressing key bottlenecks in reliability, accuracy, and user accessibility.
